Recently, hydropower was added with the Smithland Hydroelectric Plant developed by American Municipal Power (AMP) at 76 MW, coming online around 2017. Here’s a concise, comprehensive overview of Smithland Lock and Dam:

What it is
- A major navigation project on the lower Ohio River operated by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE), Louisville District.
- It creates a stable navigation pool and provides two high-capacity lock chambers for commercial tows and recreational vessels.
- The dam itself does not provide flood control; its gates are raised during high flows to pass the river.

Location
- On the Ohio River near Smithland, Kentucky (Livingston County), opposite Pope County, Illinois.
- River mile: roughly 918.5 (the Ohio River is measured from Pittsburgh; Cairo, Illinois, at the Mississippi confluence, is mile ~981).
- Close to the confluence with the Cumberland River at Smithland.

Locks and navigation features
- Two adjacent lock chambers designed for modern tows:
  - Main lock: 110 feet wide by 1,200 feet long.
  - Auxiliary lock: 110 feet wide by 1,200 feet long. 
- The dual 1,200-foot locks reduce tow delays by allowing most Ohio River tows to pass in a single lockage.
- Forms the Smithland pool upstream; downstream pool is controlled today by Olmsted Locks and Dam (which replaced the old wicket Dams 52 and 53).

Dam structure
- Concrete dam with gated spillway (tainter gates) to regulate pool elevation for navigation.
- Primary purpose is maintaining a navigable depth; not designed as a storage reservoir.

Ownership and operations
- Navigation project owner/operator: USACE, Louisville District.
- Hydropower facility (separate but integrated with the dam): owned by American Municipal Power, Inc. (AMP) on behalf of participating public power communities.

Hydropower (Smithland Hydroelectric Plant)
- Capacity: about 76 megawatts total.
- Configuration: three bulb-type Kaplan turbines (run-of-river), designed to use the dam’s existing head without impounding additional water.
- Commercial operation began in 2017.
- Provides renewable energy to AMP member communities; includes fish passage and environmental mitigation features typical of modern run-of-river installations.

History and timeline
- Built as part of the modernization of the Ohio River navigation system that replaced multiple small wicket dams dating from the early 1900s.
- Construction era: 1970s; locks and dam placed in service around 1980.
- Hydropower added decades later (licensed and constructed in the 2010s).
- Downstream system modernization: Olmsted Locks and Dam came online in the late 2010s, replacing Dams 52 and 53 and changing downstream pool management relative to Smithland.

Traffic and economic role
- Serves one of the nation’s busiest inland freight corridors, moving coal, petroleum products, aggregates, grain, chemicals, steel, and other commodities.
- The dual 1,200-foot locks accommodate the prevalent 15-barge tows on the lower Ohio, cutting transit times and reducing tow breakage.

Public access and recreation
- As with most navigation dams, restricted areas exist near the lock walls and dam for safety and security; obey USACE signage and buoy lines.
- Bank and tailwater fishing downstream can be popular (species often include catfish, sauger, and others), subject to state regulations.
- Check USACE Louisville District notices for any visitor facilities, closures, or special restrictions.

Safety notes
- Strong currents, turbulence, and rapidly changing conditions occur near the dam and in the approaches to the locks.
- Recreational boaters must monitor river stages, heed navigation lights/signals, and coordinate with lock operators via marine radio per posted procedures.

Also worth knowing
- Smithland is one of several modernized lower-Ohio projects with 1,200-foot locks: nearby peers include John T. Myers (upstream), Newburgh, and Cannelton.
- Environmental management at run-of-river hydro sites like Smithland focuses on maintaining fish habitat, minimizing entrainment, and protecting water quality while using existing navigation structures for power generation.

If you want, I can add maps, current lock status or queue info, recent tow traffic stats, or hydropower generation data.
